teaser: Everyone knows this face. Almost no one knows who is really screaming.

lesson.text: Four. That is how many Screams Edvard Munch made by hand: two paintings and two pastels, between 1893 and 1910, plus a print he could run off in black and white. One of the pastels sold in 2012 for almost 120 million dollars. This is the earliest painted one, from 1893, and the most famous.

It is also flimsier than you might guess. Munch did not use canvas. He worked on a sheet of cardboard, 91 by 73.5 centimeters (about 36 by 29 inches), with thin tempera, a fast-drying matte paint, and with crayon. In places the bare brown board shows through.

The picture began as a walk. Munch wrote it down more than once. He was going along a road above the fjord at sunset with two friends. The sky turned blood red. He stopped, exhausted, and leaned on the railing. His friends walked on.
Munch was not alone on that road. Where are his companions?

spots.title: The two friends
spots.text: Two dark figures in hats at the far end of the railing, upright as posts. They are walking away, or have not noticed anything. Whatever is happening, it is happening to one person only.

lesson.text: That distance matters, because of what Munch wrote next. Standing there, trembling with anxiety, he sensed “an infinite scream passing through nature.” Read that again. The scream is not coming out of the figure. It is coming at it.

The person in The Scream is most likely not screaming. The hands are clamped over the ears to shut out a cry that fills the sky and the water. Munch's first title, in German, meant “The Scream of Nature.”
How do you paint a sound? Munch's answer is in the construction. He builds the picture out of two kinds of line that do not belong together, and he puts the figure on the wrong side.
Two worlds share this board: one ruled, one liquid.

lines.label: The railing
lines.text: Dead straight, plunging toward the friends. Railing and planks are the man-made world: measured, solid, rational. The friends stand inside it.

lines.label: The sky
lines.text: Nothing straight up here. Bands of red, orange and a few streaks of blue-green roll sideways like sound waves.

lines.label: The fjord
lines.text: The water curls into a whirlpool and pours down the right side. Land and sea melt into one current.

lines.label: The figure
lines.text: The body has no bones. It sways in an S, like the fjord behind it. The figure stands on the bridge but is drawn in the language of the landscape.

lesson.text: So the scream has already entered the body. That is why the figure looks the way it does: Munch stripped away everything that would make it a particular person, until only the feeling was left.

lesson.title: Up close
lesson.text: Three places where you can see how little Munch needed.

spots.title: The head
spots.text: No hair, no ears, no age, no sex. Two rings for eyes, two dots for a nose, an oval for a mouth. It is nearer to a skull or a light bulb than a portrait, which is why anyone can see themselves in it.

spots.title: Two boats
spots.text: Tiny ships with masts ride at anchor on the yellow fjord. Ordinary evening life goes on down there, untroubled.

spots.title: The sky's surface
spots.text: The red is dragged on in long dry strokes, with crayon lines on top. You can count them. Munch wanted speed and rawness, not polish.

lesson.text: Some astronomers think the blood-red sky was real. In 1883 the volcano Krakatoa exploded in Indonesia, and its dust made sunsets blaze across Europe for months. Munch was 19 or 20 then. It is a theory, and others point out that he painted moods, not weather reports.

When the picture was shown in Norway, people questioned his sanity out loud. Munch came from a family marked by illness: his mother and his older sister died of tuberculosis when he was a child, and another sister was treated for mental illness. He feared madness all his life.

In the top left of the sky, someone wrote a sentence in tiny pencil letters: “Can only have been painted by a madman!” For over a century it was blamed on an angry visitor. In 2021 the museum compared the handwriting under infrared light. It is Munch's own.

Why would he write that on his own picture? Perhaps as a bitter joke at his critics, perhaps as a way of owning the insult. He never erased it. It is too faint to see in a photograph, but visitors in Oslo can look for it.

On February 12, 1994, the opening day of the Winter Olympics in Norway, two men leaned a ladder against the museum, broke a window and took this painting in under a minute. They left a note: “Thanks for the poor security.” It was recovered, unharmed, three months later.

Today the bald head with its open mouth is an emoji, a horror movie mask, a Halloween costume. Each copy borrows the face and forgets the two friends walking away. Go back to them once more. The hardest thing in this picture is not the scream. It is that nobody else hears it.

quiz.question: What is this version of The Scream painted on?
quiz.explanation: Munch used tempera and crayon on a sheet of cardboard.

quiz.question: According to Munch's own account, where does the scream come from?
quiz.explanation: He wrote of sensing an infinite scream passing through nature.

quiz.question: Who wrote the pencil sentence about a madman in the sky?
quiz.explanation: A 2021 handwriting study showed it is Munch's own.

quiz.question: How is the figure's body drawn, compared with the bridge?
options: In straight lines like the railing
In curves like the fjord and sky
It is not drawn at all
quiz.explanation: The body sways in an S, in the language of the landscape.

quiz.question: What happened to this painting in 1994?
options: It was stolen on the opening day of the Winter Olympics
It was sold for 120 million dollars
quiz.explanation: Thieves took it in under a minute and left a mocking note.

quiz.question: How many versions of The Scream did Munch make by hand?
quiz.explanation: Two paintings and two pastels, plus a print.

facts.text: The two figures in the background are running toward the screaming person to help.
facts.explanation: They stand upright at the far end of the railing and take no notice.

facts.text: One theory links the red sky to the eruption of the volcano Krakatoa.
facts.explanation: Its dust caused vivid sunsets across Europe in 1883, though the link is only a theory.

facts.text: The Scream of 1893 is an oil painting on canvas.
facts.explanation: It is tempera and crayon on cardboard.
